Abstract
Purpose: With the widespread introduction of dual energy computed tomogra-
phy (DECT), applications utilizing the spectral information to perform material
decomposition became available. Among these, a popular application is to
decompose contrast-enhanced CT images into virtual non-contrast (VNC) or
virtual non-iodine images and into iodine maps. In 2021, photon-counting CT
(PCCT) was introduced,which is another spectral CT modality.It allows for scans
with more than two different detected spectra. With these systems, it becomes
possible to distinguish more than two materials. It is frequently proposed to
administer more than one contrast agent, perform a single PCCT scan, and
then calculate the VNC images and the contrast agent maps. This may not be
optimal because the patient is injected with a material, only to have it computa-
tionally extracted again immediately afterwards by spectral CT. It may be better
to do an unenhanced scan followed by one or more contrast-enhanced scans.
The main argument for the spectral material decomposition is patient motion,
which poses a signiﬁcant challenge for approaches involving two or more tem-
porally separated scans.In this work,we assume that we can correct for patient
motion and thus are free to scan the patient more than once.Our goal is then to
quantify the penalty for performing a single contrast-enhanced scan rather than
a clever series of unenhanced and enhanced scans. In particular, we consider
the impact on patient dose and image quality.
Methods: We simulate CT scans of three differently sized phantoms containing
various contrast agents.We do this for a variety of tube voltage settings,a variety
of patient-speciﬁc preﬁlter (PSP) thicknesses and a variety of threshold settings
of the photon-counting detector with up to four energy bins. The reconstructed
bin images give the expectation values of soft tissue and of the contrast agents.
Error propagation of projection noise into the images yields the image noise.
Dose is quantiﬁed using the total CT dose index (CTDI) value of the scans.
When combining multiple scans,we further consider all possible tube current (or
dose) ratios between the scans. Material decomposition is done image-based
in a statistical optimal way. Error propagation into the material-speciﬁc images
yields the signal-to-noise ratio at unit dose (SNRD). The winning scan strategy
is the one with the highest total SNRD, which is related to the SNRD of the
material that has the lowest signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) among the materials to
decompose into. We consider scan strategies with up to three scans and up to
three materials (water W, contrast agent X and contrast agent Y).

Results: In all cases, those scan strategies yield the best performance that
combine differently enhanced scans, for example, W+WX, W+WXY, WX+WXY,
W+WX+WY, with W denoting an unenhanced scan and WX, WY and WXY
denoting X–, Y–, and X–Y–enhanced scans, respectively. The dose efﬁciency
of scans with a single enhancement scheme, such as WX or WXY, is far lower.
The dose penalty to pay for these single enhancement strategies is about two or
greater. Our ﬁndings also apply to scans with a single energy bin and thus also
to CT systems with conventional, energy-integrating detectors, that is, conven-
tional DECT. Dual source CT (DSCT) scans are preferable over single source
CT scans, also because one can use a PSP on the high Kilovolt spectrum to
better separate the detected spectra. For the strategies and tasks considered
here, it does not make sense to simultaneously scan with two different types of
contrast agents. Iodine outperforms other high Z elements in nearly all cases.
Conclusions: Given the signiﬁcant dose penalty when performing only one
contrast–enhanced scan rather than a series of unenhanced and enhanced
scans, one should consider avoiding the single–scan strategies. This requires
to invest in the development of accurate registration algorithms that can
compensate for patient and contrast agent motion between separate scans.

INTRODUCTION
Dual energy CT (DECT) is a wide-spread spectral imag-
ing modality that is typically realized using dual source
CT, fast tube voltage switching, sandwich detectors or
split preﬁltration.1 In 2021, photon-counting CT (PCCT)
was introduced as another spectral imaging modality.
The photon-counting detectors have the inherent capa-
bility to provide a better iodine contrast,2–8 distinguish
photon energies and see two or more detected spectra
simultaneously.9–12 Their ability to discriminate between
different photon energies makes the use of other
high-Z elements as contrast agents promising.13–17 A
detailed technological overview of the corresponding
clinical CT technology can be found in references
18–20. A very typical application for spectral CT is the
decomposition of a contrast-enhanced CT scan into
a nonenhanced image and a contrast agent map. The
simultaneous administration of more than one contrast
agent for PCCT with more than two detected spectra is
highly debated9,13,21–36 and probably not performed in
patients only because there is no approval of relevant
contrast agents other than iodine.Ideally,one would use
different contrast agent molecules that have different
pharmacokinetic proﬁles and thus distribute differently
in the body. They could be injected simultaneously or
consecutively while a subsequent CT scan that simulta-
neously images the bolus of all contrast agents would
reveal the contrast agent distribution for each of the two
molecule types.
The principle of spectral CT is that the CT value of
the contrast agent, say X, changes with the spectrum
used, while the CT value of water, and soft tissue,
remains constant, due to the water precorrection. With
at least two different detected spectra, it is therefore
possible to compute a material-selective image. For
example, a simple subtraction cancels out the soft
tissue, leaving only the contrast agent map. Two such
acquisitions can typically be performed simultaneously,
either with conventional detectors using dual source CT
or fast tube voltage switching, or with energy-selective
detectors, or with a combination of both. With WX+WX,
where W stands for water or soft tissue, we denote
two X-enhanced scans with potentially different emitted
x-ray spectra and energy-integrating or photon-counting
detectors (refer to Table 2 for the scan notation used in
this paper). Such scans would be carried out preferably
simultaneously, for example, with dual source CT or
with fast tube voltage switching, with the patient being
in the same contrast enhancement phase. With WX
we denote a single X-enhanced scan. To distinguish
between soft tissue and contrast agent, WX requires
energy-selective detectors, such as dual layer detectors
or photon-counting detectors.
However, it would be better to combine an unen-
hanced scan with a contrast-enhanced scan. Between
such two scans the change of the CT value in a
contrast-enhanced region is much higher than for any
combination of detected spectra in a single scan.Hence,
the contrast-to-noise ratio for a given total dose level will
be signiﬁcantly higher. The downside of this two-scan
strategy, which we denote as W+WX, is that the scans
cannot be carried out simultaneously. W+WX can be
regarded a temporal subtraction technique, as opposed
to an energy subtraction technique as used for the WX
scan strategy.

With W+WX, patient motion becomes a challenge:
motion leads to inconsistent patient positions between
the two scans and it becomes impossible to retrieve
the iodine map just by subtracting the unenhanced
scan from the contrast-enhanced scan. Sophisticated
deformable registration techniques might remedy this
problem to some extent. One of the early approaches
for deformable registration is the Demons algorithm37
and its diffeomorphic extension.38 These are orig-
inally intended for monomodal registration, that is,
for images with the same gray value scale. Regis-
tration approaches for multi- or cross-modal image
registration have been proposed early as well, for
example, by histogram adaptation39 or by maximiz-
ing cross-correlation.40 Another classical registration
approach is the dense displacement sampling (DEEDS)
algorithm.41,42 Notably, mutual information-based met-
rics were used to tackle the dual energy registration
problem in a classical way43 and by using a neural
network.44 Important neural network-based registration
approaches to mention are the VoxelMorph algorithm45
and further developments.46,47 Simulations and patient
studies suggest that pre- and post-contrast lung acquisi-
tions can and should be registered with sub-voxel accu-
racy.However,residual errors may still negatively impact
the accuracy of iodine map calculations and exacer-
bate beam-hardening artifacts.48–50 Recently, also style
transfer neural networks have been proposed to trans-
fer the spectral information from one image to another
without a need for highly accurate registration between
them.51,52 With such algorithms,motion between the two
scans of W+WX might no longer be a problem.Although
this is not yet proven, we here want to assume that
patient or contrast agent motion is a problem that can
be solved. This allows us to ignore the motion problem
and investigate the potential dose beneﬁts.
Similar observations regarding the advantages of
temporal subtraction over energy subtraction have
already been made in the ﬁeld of digital subtraction
angiography (DSA): DSA is a temporal x-ray image
subtraction technique of type W+WX where the unen-
hanced x-ray image, the so-called mask, is subtracted
from the X-enhanced x-ray image in order to obtain
an iodine only x-ray image, the so-called DSA image.
Motion has always been a problem with DSA and, thus,
dual energy subtraction techniques (DESA) have been
proposed where WX is decomposed into an iodine map
by the use of, for example, fast tube voltage switch-
ing research C-arm systems (where it was found that
an additional deformable registration step is neces-
sary to account for small patient movements between
each image frame pair53). Moreover, hybrid techniques,
combining the temporal subtraction with the energy sub-
traction, using the W+WX strategy in combination with
fast tube voltage switching, have been analyzed. The
main ﬁndings were that WX could only be as good
as W+WX if better detectors were available and, even
then, the hybrid option is the best.54,55 While the tem-
poral subtraction, that is, the classical DSA, is routine
practice in the clinic for decades, DESA techniques
have never resulted in a clinical product, the main rea-
son being the increased noise and the resulting poor
image quality. Another reason may be that dual energy
acquisition hardware was not available in clinical C-arm
systems. Instead of using spectral techniques vendors
rather try to reduce DSA’s motion problem by register-
ing the mask to the current image, for example, using
pixel shifts,afﬁne or deformable registrations.After such
motion compensation the actual DSA subtraction takes
place.
While one may agree that perfectly compensating
for potential motion between CT scans in a multiphase
acquisition is valuable,multiphasic scans are being suc-
cessfully used in clinical routine, today. The lack of
perfectly registered images does not appear to be a
major challenge for this technique. This is because
the multiphasic scans are treated independently from
each other, for example, the three-phase liver proto-
col is W, WX, WX (unenhanced, followed by arterial
enhancement, followed by the portal venous phase,
sometimes even followed by a fourth scan to measure
the late enhancement), with X = iodine. With such pro-
tocols no material decomposition is possible due to
patient motion, unless energy-selective detectors are
being used. If there was no motion, protocols such as
W+WX+WX may become possible, with a signiﬁcant
dose beneﬁt, as will be shown.
Similarly,when using two contrast agents,say,X and Y,
it might not be the best idea to administer them simulta-
neously to perform one CT scan.Reference 56 analyzed
the noise increase inherent in increasing the dimen-
sionality of material decomposition: The more materials
need to be decomposed, the higher the required dose.
Instead of using X and Y simultaneously, it might
thus be better to perform one CT scan WX with con-
trast agent X and a second CT scan WY using contrast
agent Y. This means WX+WY or WX, WY. References
57, 58 show in phantom studies with PCCT and dual-
source DECT, respectively, that two separate scans,
WX, WY, clearly outperform a single double-enhanced
scan WXY. Double-enhanced multi-energy scans, that
is, WXY, that make either use of four energy thresholds
(in the research PCCT) or of two different tube volt-
ages (in the DSCT with the conventional detectors) are
compared with two independent single energy scans.
The authors’two-scan experiments use both scans com-
pletely independently from each other, which in our
notation is given by WX,WY.Since references 57,58 are
of experimental nature, there were a lot of aspects the
authors could not include but which we will investigate
here: (a) combine the information from the two sepa-
rate scans (such as WX+WY), (b) use more than one
tube voltage for the PCCT scans, (c) use more than two
energy bins (or thresholds), (d) combine unenhanced

While simultaneous multicontrast imaging is an attrac-
tive application to demonstrate the technical capability
of PCCT, it is not our intent to make claims whether
simultaneously scanning a second contrast agent would
be of any help or not. There are several clinical
multiple contrast agent examples discussed in the
literature.9,13,21–36 For example, biphasic liver imaging
could be done in one scan with iodine and gadolin-
ium. Similarly, endoleaks are characterized by arterial
and venous or delayed phase CT imaging and instead
of multiple CT scans one might consider using multi-
ple contrast agents. Small bowel imaging may beneﬁt
from visualizing the arterial enhancement of iodine in
the vascularized bowel wall and bismuth that enhances
the intestinal lumen, which could be done in a single
CT scan. The decomposition of, for example, a coro-
nary, into calciﬁed plaque and iodine-enhanced lumen
is discussed as well and ﬁts into our discussion when
regarding the calcium as a second contrast agent (that,
however, cannot be removed). Also, the characterization
of tumor vasculature, for example, using gold nanopar-
ticles combined with an iodinated contrast agent is
discussed. All of these examples are nice and may be
clinically relevant.However,they may not really require a
simultaneous scan and could be potentially replaced by
two adjacent CT scans.Moreover,some of the examples
require two different contrast agents if and only if these
shall be assessed in a single CT scan (Table 1).
In some of these examples there appears to be
no clinical need of a second contrast agent. More-
over, no such high-Z agents are clinically available. The
availability today is restricted to barium and iodine. Bar-
ium is administered orally, and iodine is administered
intravenously. Gadolinium is available for magnetic res-
onance imaging at concentrations far too low to make a
good CT contrast. Our aim is to clearly state the penal-
ties (e.g., in terms of dose) associated with using more
than one contrast agent simultaneously. We also want
to quantify the differences in image quality or patient
dose between the conventional approach of a single
enhanced CT scan and propose alternative multiple-
scan strategies (for single- or multi-contrast imaging).
We further intend to promote those strategies that also
contain an unenhanced scan, since these turn out to be
particularly dose-efﬁcient,even though they may require
patient motion compensation.
The paper is organized as follows. In a ﬁrst step, we
introduce the notation used to deﬁne the scan strate-
gies. Then, we describe the simulation, the material
decomposition algorithm and the ﬁgure of merit used
for evaluation. What follows are the numerical experi-
ments carried out and, ﬁnally, the results in terms of the
ﬁgure of merit and in terms of dose (penalties). The
optimal scan parameters themselves, due to the vast
amount, are given in the appendix, which is found in the
supporting material.

SCAN STRATEGY NOTATION
A scan strategy is a single CT scan or a series of two
or more CT scans of the same patient used to fulﬁll a
material decomposition task. A scan is either W (unen-
hanced), WX (X-enhanced, with contrast agent X), WY
(Y-enhanced) or WXY (double enhanced, two contrast
agents used simultaneously). Our notation only shows
the enhancement status of the patient. It does not show
the scan parameters (tube current,tube voltage,preﬁlter
thickness, detector bin settings). These are determined
using the optimization strategy introduced below. The
thus-determined optimal scan parameters are listed in
the appendix.
If the scan strategy consists of more than one scan,
a plus sign between the scans indicates that these
scans are perfectly aligned,either due to the absence of
motion (e.g.,when both scans are conducted simultane-
ously) or algorithmic motion compensation. Thus, scans
connected with a plus sign can be used for joint material
decomposition. In contrast, a comma sign indicates that
there is motion (that is not or cannot be compensated
for) and each scan of the respective scan strategy thus
needs to be used independently. Multiphasic liver scans

MATERIALS AND METHODS
3.1
Simulations
To mimic the attenuation properties of patients we sim-
ulate rawdata of a circular phantom in three different
sizes: small (S, 20 cm), medium (M, 30 cm), and large
(L, 40 cm). We may refer to the phantoms as patients,
below. Each phantom contains a central 1 cm lesion
that can be ﬁlled with contrast agents. The dilution of
the contrast agents with water is chosen such that
the diluted contrast agent would have a CT value of
200 HU if placed in the center of a 32 cm water phan-
tom and scanned with a 120 kV spectrum with intrinsic
preﬁltration (but without additional patient-speciﬁc pre-
ﬁltration). This deﬁnition is independent of the patient
size and the actual x-ray spectra used for the sim-
ulated scans. The value of 200 HU was chosen as
typical to the enhancement of today’s iodinated contrast
agents. It is high enough to provide a good enhance-
ment and small enough not to signiﬁcantly inﬂuence the
patient’s total attenuation and image noise.The contrast
agents of potential interest are iodine, gadolinium, ytter-
bium, hafnium, tungsten, gold, and bismuth. However,
the vast amount of combinations leads to signiﬁcant
compute times of our optimization making the amount
of generated data quite large and hard to present. We
therefore restrict our considerations to iodine, gadolin-
ium, hafnium, and bismuth. The K-edges of these four
materials are at 33.2, 50.2, 65.4, and 90.5 keV, respec-
tively, covering a wide range of energies. Depending on
the x-ray spectrum, preﬁltration, phantom size, detec-
tor bin settings, and other factors, these materials will
show an individual enhancement, different from above’s
200 HU.
Our simulations use the Tucker x-ray spectrum
model59 with a 7◦anode angle, preﬁltered by 6 mm alu-
minum as inherent preﬁltration.The tube voltages range
from 70 to 150 kV in steps of 10 kV. We further simulate
patient-speciﬁc copper preﬁlters (PSP) of thicknesses
0, 1, 2, and 3 mm, that could be inserted or removed
before the scan by the help of a ﬁlter change mecha-
nism. The 2 mm Cu preﬁlter approximately correspond
to a 0.6 mm tin preﬁlter or a 0.5 mm silver preﬁlter. Tin
is the ﬁlter material used in patient-speciﬁc preﬁltration
in all Siemens CT systems, and silver is a PSP mate-
rial used in some Canon scanners. The K-edges of tin
(29.2 keV) and silver (25.5 keV) are close to the K-
edge of iodine (33.2 keV) which makes them suboptimal
choices for dose reduction for iodine-enhanced scans as
long as tube voltages below 70 kV are not available.60
Therefore,to be vendor-agnostic,we decided to use cop-
per instead. Its K-edge (8.9 keV) is outside the energy
range relevant for diagnostic CT.
As detector material we assume a cadmium telluride
(CdTe) detector with 1.6 mm sensor thickness and an
ideal energy response (rectangular energy bins) as well
as a realistic energy response taken from reference
61. The ideal energy response is chosen to obtain
the most conservative comparison between a single
scan with multiple contrast agents and multiple scans
with and without contrast agents. The single scan will
generally beneﬁt from the ideal detector response
more signiﬁcantly than the multiple-scan strategies, as
the latter allow for individual adjustments of the tube
voltage, tube current, and preﬁlter thickness. The detec-
tor’s energy threshold positions that we consider are at
{20, 33.2, 50.2, 61.3, 65.4, 69.5, 80.7, 90.5, 100, 120} keV
with the non-integer numbers corresponding to the
K-edges of iodine, gadolinium, ytterbium, hafnium, tung-
sten, gold, and bismuth, respectively, some of which are
discussed as potential contrast agents of interest for
diagnostic CT. For a given tube voltage U, only thresh-

For all contrast agent combinations and scan strate-
gies we want to ﬁnd the optimal scan mode, that is, the
scan mode that yields the highest SNRD. In our simula-
tion,we measure the signal as the CT value of an Region
of Interest (ROI) in the enhanced (or unenhanced) cen-
tral 1 cm lesion of our phantom. Noise is given as the
standard deviation of the same ROI.The corresponding
noise variance is calculated by error propagation of the
projection variances through the ﬁltered backprojection
algorithm into the image domain. The standard devia-
tion results as the square-root of the thus-calculated
variance. Dose is calculated as the weighted CT dose
index (CTDI) value using a simulated water-equivalent
32 cm CTDI phantom.The CTDI values were calculated
as follows:We performed Monte Carlo simulations (with
our in-house Monte Carlo simulation that provides dose
and scatter distributions62) as well as analytical calcula-
tions (energy absorbed within the phantom). We found
the relative errors between the two methods to be less
than 4%, whereby the Monte Carlo simulations were
noisy and the analytical ones were not. We then chose
to use the noise-free analytical values.To optimize com-
pute performance, a list of intermediate CTDI values is
calculated assuming monochromatic x-rays at each kilo-
electronvolts step ranging from 1 to 150 keV. For a given
x-ray spectrum (tube voltage, preﬁlter) the correspond-

the precalculated single kiloelectronvolts CTDI values,

4.1
One contrast agent
We analyze the case of administering one contrast
agent, as it is done in CT, today. Thus, we decompose
into the M = 2 materials water (W) and iodine (X).Three
strategies to achieve this are of interest.
WX One contrast-enhanced scan, for example,
with photon-counting detectors, with B ≥2
bins.
WX+WX two contrast-enhanced scans. This is the

W+WX one unenhanced scan followed by an X-

Apart from iodine, high-Z contrast agents with K-
edges above 50 keV are of interest, for example as a
replacement for iodine.Such contrast agents could offer
advantages to patients with known reactions to iodine.
However, there are no clinical studies supporting this.
Even the opposite may be the case. For example, con-
sider gadolinium which has known problems in terms of
patient safety.64 Nevertheless, having a high-Z element
with a K-edge at a rather high energy,such as 60–80 keV,
can give more ﬂexibility in tube voltage selection since it
does not require the tube voltage to be as low as possi-
ble, as is the case with iodine, today. Adipose or obese
patients might beneﬁt from this increase in tube voltage.
Moreover, one threshold of the photon-counting detec-
tor can be placed right at that K-edge to maximize the
achievable contrast.
In addition to iodine, we therefore also analyze the
properties of other high-Z materials in this work.

preferable to combine one unenhanced scan W with

highest SNRD,result from scan strategies that also con-

involve iodine as the only agent perform very well. We
also see that the strategies with two independent scans
(with uncorrectable motion) are on par with or even
outperform the strategies with two contrast agents that
do not include an unenhanced scan. Table 13 lists the

phantom size it is likely that they generalize to other
phantom and patient shapes since those,for example,of
oval or elliptical shaped cross-sections, can be thought

Assuming that other possible material decomposition
algorithms also do their decomposition in a statistically
optimal way and do not implement algorithmic means of
reducing image noise,there will be no general difference
in the results. Even those algorithms that do a nonlin-
ear decomposition in rawdata domain,as opposed to our
linear approach will be identical to ours and differ only
in second order effects. Noise reduction approaches, as
they could be implemented by rawdata postprocessing,
iterative reconstruction, or artiﬁcial intelligence-based
processing,can be applied to all approaches and should
not enter our discussion at all, since we only focus on
the physics aspects of material decomposition. A fair
noise reduction applied equally to all approaches will be
of equal beneﬁt to all approaches and therefore cannot
reverse our ﬁndings.We are therefore conﬁdent that our
ﬁndings generalize very well to other objects, scanners
and algorithms even though the given SNRD values are
those of our phantoms, scanner, and algorithm and will
certainly differ somewhat from situation to situation.
There are several limitations to our work. First, we
present a simulation study only.Second,the task that we
have analyzed here is material decomposition, mean-
ing that we only consider the image quality of the VNC
image and of the contrast agent maps. Material decom-
position is the most challenging task in terms of noise
ampliﬁcation. Other, less demanding, tasks remain to be
analyzed. One such task heavily used today is contrast
maximization instead of material decomposition. For
this task, the spectral information of the acquired data
is used to maximize the CNRD between the contrast-
enhanced regions and the surrounding unenhanced
regions. Our ﬁndings, which are relevant for material
decomposition, do not necessarily apply to the contrast
maximization task. Another task that is related to mate-
rial decomposition but not considered in this work is
the decomposition of vessels into calciﬁed plaques and
contrast-enhanced lumen. Using iodine as a contrast
agent, this task is challenging due to the similar energy
dependence of the photon attenuation of calcium and
iodine in the relevant energy range. It is expected that
other elements, such as gadolinium, hafnium, tungsten
or bismuth would outperform iodine for this speciﬁc task.
In summary, our study shows the signiﬁcant dose (or
image quality) beneﬁt that can be obtained from combin-
ing an unenhanced with one or more enhanced scans.

Abstract: Purpose: With the widespread introduction of dual energy computed tomogra- phy (DECT), applications utilizing the spectral information to perform material decomposition became available. Among these, a popular application is to decompose contrast-enhanced CT images into virtual non-contrast (VNC) or virtual non-iodine images and into iodine maps. In 2021, photon-counting CT (PCCT) was introduced,which is another spectral CT modality.It allows for scans with more than two different detected spectra. With these systems, it becomes possible to distinguish more than two materials. It is frequently proposed to administer more than one contrast agent, perform a single PCCT scan, and then calculate the VNC images and the contrast agent maps. This may not be optimal because the patient is injected with a material, only to have it computa- tionally extracted again immediately afterwards by spectral CT. It may be better to do an unenhanced scan followed by one or more contrast-enhanced scans. The main argument for the spectral material decomposition is patient motion, which poses a signiﬁcant challenge for approaches involving two or more tem- porally separated scans.In this work,we assume that we can correct for patient motion and thus are free to scan the patient more than once.Our goal is then to quantify the penalty for performing a single contrast-enhanced scan rather than a clever series of unenhanced and enhanced scans. In particular, we consider the impact on patient dose and image quality. Methods: We simulate CT scans of three differently sized phantoms containing various contrast agents.We do this for a variety of tube voltage settings,a variety of patient-speciﬁc preﬁlter (PSP) thicknesses and a variety of threshold settings of the photon-counting detector with up to four energy bins. The reconstructed bin images give the expectation values of soft tissue and of the contrast agents. Error propagation of projection noise into the images yields the image noise. Dose is quantiﬁed using the total CT dose index (CTDI) value of the scans. When combining multiple scans,we further consider all possible tube current (or dose) ratios between the scans. Material decomposition is done image-based in a statistical optimal way. Error propagation into the material-speciﬁc images yields the signal-to-noise ratio at unit dose (SNRD). The winning scan strategy is the one with the highest total SNRD, which is related to the SNRD of the material that has the lowest signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) among the materials to decompose into. We consider scan strategies with up to three scans and up to three materials (water W, contrast agent X and contrast agent Y). Results: In all cases, those scan strategies yield the best performance that combine differently enhanced scans, for example, W+WX, W+WXY, WX+WXY, W+WX+WY, with W denoting an unenhanced scan and WX, WY and WXY denoting X–, Y–, and X–Y–enhanced scans, respectively. The dose efﬁciency of scans with a single enhancement scheme, such as WX or WXY, is far lower. The dose penalty to pay for these single enhancement strategies is about two or greater. Our ﬁndings also apply to scans with a single energy bin and thus also to CT systems with conventional, energy-integrating detectors, that is, conven- tional DECT. Dual source CT (DSCT) scans are preferable over single source CT scans, also because one can use a PSP on the high Kilovolt spectrum to better separate the detected spectra. For the strategies and tasks considered here, it does not make sense to simultaneously scan with two different types of contrast agents. Iodine outperforms other high Z elements in nearly all cases. Conclusions: Given the signiﬁcant dose penalty when performing only one contrast–enhanced scan rather than a series of unenhanced and enhanced scans, one should consider avoiding the single–scan strategies. This requires to invest in the development of accurate registration algorithms that can compensate for patient and contrast agent motion between separate scans.
